title: Why the Two Halves Are One Theorem

steps.body:
Part 1: **differentiating an accumulation gives back the function.** (A′ = f)
Part 2: **the accumulation can be computed from any antiderivative.** (∫ₐᵇ f = F(b) − F(a))

These are not two facts. They are one fact, read in two directions: **differentiation and integration are inverse operations.** Part 2 is what you get by taking Part 1 seriously.

explanationVariants: A(x) = ∫ₐˣ f has A′ = f (Part 1), so A is an antiderivative. Any other antiderivative F differs by a constant, so F(b) − F(a) = A(b) − A(a) = A(b) − 0 = ∫ₐᵇ f.
The whole of Part 2 is three moves: A is an antiderivative; constants cancel in a subtraction; A(a) = 0.

widget.prompt: Put the derivation of Part 2 in order.

items.label: Constants cancel in a subtraction, so F(b) − F(a) = A(b) − A(a)
A(x) = ∫ₐˣ f has A′ = f, so A is an antiderivative of f (Part 1)
A(a) = 0, so A(b) − A(a) = A(b) = ∫ₐᵇ f
Any other antiderivative F differs from A by a constant

misorderFeedback.feedback: You cannot say the constants cancel before establishing that two antiderivatives DIFFER by a constant.
A(a) = 0 is the last step, not the first. Begin with Part 1: A is an antiderivative.

widget.missFeedback: Start with Part 1 (A is an antiderivative), then the constant, then the cancellation, then A(a) = 0.
widget.successFeedback: Four moves, and Part 2 falls out of Part 1. They were never two theorems.

widget.prompt: f(x) = 2x. Sweep out an area of 9, and read BOTH theorems off the same picture.
widget.successFeedback: x = 3, area 9. Part 1 is the tangent line: the slope of A at x = 3 is 6, which is the height of f. Part 2 is the value: A(3) = 9, which is F(3) − F(0) with F(x) = x². Same picture, same sweep — one theorem, read either as a statement about slopes or as a statement about values.
widget.lowFeedback: Not enough area. Keep sweeping right.

predict.prompt: You'll sweep out area under f(x) = 2x from the left. As x moves right, the accumulated area grows…
predict.reveal: Area pours in at exactly the current height of f(x) = 2x — and that height keeps rising, so the accumulation curve bends upward. The rate the area grows IS the function's height.

cml.actionGoal: Move an upper bound and coordinate accumulated area with the integrand's current value.

explanationVariants: Differentiating an integral is Part 1. Evaluating an integral with an antiderivative is Part 2.
Part 1 is a statement about slopes; Part 2 is a recipe for values.

widget.prompt: Which half of the theorem does each task use?

items.label: Find d/dx[∫₂ˣ sin t dt]
items.feedback: Differentiating an accumulation — Part 1 hands back the integrand: sin x.

items.label: Compute ∫₀¹ x⁵ dx
items.feedback: Finding a VALUE from an antiderivative: F(x) = x⁶/6, so the answer is 1/6.

items.label: Find where ∫₀ˣ (t − 5) dt is smallest
items.feedback: Turning points of an accumulation need its DERIVATIVE, which Part 1 says is the integrand. Set t − 5 = 0.

items.label: Find the total water from a flow rate over [0, 4]
items.feedback: A definite total from a rate — antiderivative, then subtract.

widget.missFeedback: Are you DIFFERENTIATING an integral (Part 1) or EVALUATING one (Part 2)?
widget.successFeedback: Differentiate an accumulation → Part 1. Compute a definite value → Part 2. One theorem, two jobs.

steps.body:
And now the two courses are one course.

Every derivative rule you learned in C1 is now an **antiderivative rule**, read backwards. The power rule reversed gives xⁿ⁺¹/(n+1). The chain rule reversed is about to give you substitution.

Differentiation was never a separate subject. It was the other half of this one.

explanationVariants: (x⁴)′ = 4x³, so an antiderivative of x³ is x⁴/4. Check by differentiating: (x⁴/4)′ = x³ ✓.
Raise the power by one, then divide by the new power — the power rule, run in reverse.

widget.prompt: ∫₀² x³ dx. (An antiderivative of x³ is x⁴/4.)

commonErrors.feedback: That is 2⁴ = 16 — you evaluated x⁴ but forgot to divide by 4.
That is 2³, the height of f at the endpoint, not the area under it.
Check the antiderivative: x⁴/4 at x = 2 is 16/4 = 4, and at 0 it is 0.

hints: G(x) = ∫₀ˣ (t² − 4) dt. To find where G is smallest, you need G′ — and Part 1 tells you what that is without computing anything.
G′(x) = x² − 4, which is zero at x = 2 (in [0, 3]) and changes from negative to positive there.
Now use Part 2 to get the VALUE: an antiderivative of t² − 4 is t³/3 − 4t.
explanationVariants: One theorem, both jobs: it located the minimum AND evaluated it, and you never drew a rectangle.

widget.prompt: G(x) = ∫₀ˣ (t² − 4) dt on [0, 3]. Find the MINIMUM VALUE of G, as a decimal to three places.

commonErrors.feedback: That is WHERE the minimum occurs (x = 2), not its value. Now evaluate: G(2) = 8/3 − 8 = −5.333.
G(0) = 0, but G then goes negative — the integrand is negative on (0, 2), so area is being subtracted.
The sign is wrong. The region up to x = 2 lies BELOW the axis, so G(2) is negative: −16/3.

takeaways: Part 1 (A′ = f) and Part 2 (∫ₐᵇ f = F(b) − F(a)) are one fact: differentiation and integration are inverse.
Part 2 falls out of Part 1 in four lines — A is an antiderivative, constants cancel, A(a) = 0.
Every derivative rule is now an antiderivative rule, read backwards.
steps.teaser: Still to come in this course: the full antiderivative library, and substitution — the chain rule run in reverse.

concept.body: Ask what you are being asked to DO. Differentiating an accumulation? That is Part 1, and the answer is the integrand. Computing a definite value? That is Part 2: antiderivative, then subtract.

explanationVariants: Differentiating an integral is Part 1, and it hands the integrand straight back: x⁴.
No computation is needed — that is the point of Part 1.

options.label: x⁴
options.feedback: Right — Part 1: the derivative undoes the accumulation.

options.label: x⁵/5
options.feedback: That is the accumulation itself. Differentiating it takes you back to x⁴.
